How verification splits three ways

the distinction matters, and collapsing it would be the loophole

prose 669 claims

A human wrote sentences, a model quoted one, and the quote is string-matched against the document it came from. This is where fabrication is possible and where matching earns its keep — a range assembled from two different sentences reads perfectly and is not what the company said.

structured 2 claims

The quote is the tagged fact itself, rendered by a source adapter from a typed response. There is no prose to match, and that is not a loophole: the value came from the adapter and never from a model.

derived 0 claims

Figures the pipeline computed. Deliberately in neither set: a derived number is only as good as its inputs and must be justified by the claims underneath it rather than by its own existence.

Point-in-time enforcement

Two independent locks. Each adapter filters on the filing date, and the chain re-checks everything returned — the second lock catches an adapter that forgets, which is the bug the guard exists for. A test trips it with a document filed one day after the lock date. The retrieval window for web research is bounded at the API itself, so an article published after the lock date cannot enter the result set at all rather than being filtered afterwards. The market adapter refuses a historical as-of date outright, because serving today's consensus for a past quarter is lookahead that would surface as skill.

News is deliberately not evidence

We hold a snippet rather than the article, so matching a quote against the snippet would be circular. Coverage stays on the dossier, feeds perception only, and no lens can cite it. Retrieved research is different: its full text is written to disk as a document, so a quote against it is verified exactly like a quote from an 8-K.
